introduction-the-art-of-hiding-complexit.core: Platform engineers turn chaotic infrastructure (Kubernetes, cloud networking, IAM) into simple, safe interfaces. Good abstractions hide the details developers don't need, while letting them reach down when they must.

first_principles.problem: Developers face hundreds of Kubernetes fields and cloud options to deploy a simple service.
truths: Most developers need a few common capabilities.
Every exposed option is a decision to make.

analogy.title: A car's controls
analogy.story: Steering, pedals and a dashboard hide the engine's complexity, yet a mechanic can still open the bonnet.
analogy.breaks: Over-abstraction frustrates experts and hides problems.

example.title: A deployment, before and after
flow: After: 15-line service spec (name, image, port, replicas)

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Simple for most people, powerful when needed.

example.outcome: interfaces that match how developers think.

check.q: What's a platform engineer's core abstraction goal?
check.a: To hide complexity developers don't need while still allowing them to reach the underlying layer when necessary.

the-law-of-leaky-abstractions.core: Joel Spolsky: all non-trivial abstractions leak. Underlying details (network failures, resource limits, timeouts) eventually show through, so platforms must expect leaks rather than promise perfect black boxes.

first_principles.problem: A 'simple' platform hides everything until a pod gets OOM-killed, and developers have no idea why or where to look.
truths: Underlying systems fail in ways abstractions don't model.
Hidden details become mysteries when they leak.
derivation: **Document** what the abstraction does under the hood.

analogy.title: A garden hose
analogy.story: Usually it just delivers water, but kinks, pressure drops and leaks expose the plumbing beneath.
analogy.breaks: Exposing everything defeats the purpose, so leak information selectively.

example.title: An OOM leak
flow: Platform CLI says: 'Your service exceeded 512Mi. Raise memory in service.yaml or check for a leak.'

check.q: What does the Law of Leaky Abstractions state?
check.a: All non-trivial abstractions eventually expose details of the systems they hide.

the-law-of-leaky-abstractions-continued.core: Design for leaks with observability escape hatches (raw logs, events, metrics), progressive disclosure (simple by default, advanced options available), override mechanisms, and clear error translation, so developers can diagnose and handle the edge cases.

first_principles.problem: When something goes wrong underneath, developers are stuck because the platform gives them no way to see or adjust it.
derivation: Offer **observability hatches**: kubectl access, raw events and logs.
Provide **overrides**: patches or raw manifests for exceptions.

analogy.title: An automatic car with a manual mode
analogy.story: Drive automatically day to day, but shift to manual on a steep mountain road.
analogy.breaks: Too many overrides fragment the platform, so track their usage and absorb the common ones.

example.title: Progressive disclosure in a service spec

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Simple for 90% of cases, flexible for the other 10%.

code.text:
service: payments
image: ghcr.io/acme/payments:1.4
port: 8080
# advanced (optional)
resources: { memory: 1Gi }
overrides:
  kubernetes:
    podSpec: { priorityClassName: high }

check.q: What is progressive disclosure in platform API design?
check.a: Showing simple defaults first while making advanced options available when needed.

golden-paths-the-paved-road.core: A golden path is the opinionated, well-supported way to build and run a type of service (template + CI + deploy + observability + security). It's made so easy that people choose it, but it isn't mandatory: off-road is allowed, just less supported.

first_principles.problem: Mandates create resentment, and with no guidance every team reinvents everything differently.
derivation: **Design** paths for the common service types.

analogy.title: A paved road through a park
analogy.story: Most walkers use it because it's smooth and clear; hikers can still go off-trail at their own effort.
analogy.breaks: Golden paths can ossify, so evolve them with user feedback.

example.title: A golden path for Go services
flow: CI with tests, SAST, image signing

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: 90% of new services follow it voluntarily.

example.outcome: best practice by default, not decree.

check.q: How does a golden path differ from a mandate?
check.a: It's the easiest, best-supported option that teams choose voluntarily, with deviation allowed at their own cost.

designing-for-safety-guardrails-vs-gates.core: Gates block progress until someone approves it (manual reviews, tickets). Guardrails let teams move freely within safe boundaries enforced automatically (policy-as-code, defaults, limits). Guardrails scale; gates create queues.

first_principles.problem: A security approval gate on every deploy creates a two-day queue, so teams find ways around it.
truths: Automated checks are consistent and fast.
derivation: Give **fast feedback** in CI, not after deploy.
Keep **human gates** only for high-risk exceptions.

analogy.title: Motorway crash barriers vs. toll booths
analogy.story: Barriers keep everyone safe at full speed; toll booths stop every car.
analogy.breaks: Some decisions (production data access) still deserve human review.

example.title: Converting a gate
flow: Before: security reviews every deploy (2 days)
After: CI policy checks (image signed, no root, no public S3)

check.q: Why do guardrails scale better than gates?
check.a: They enforce safety automatically and continuously, without manual approval queues.

designing-for-safety-guardrails-vs-gates.core: Effective guardrails are layered: secure defaults (safe out of the box), preventive policies (block clearly bad configs at admission or CI), detective controls (alert on drift) and corrective automation (auto-fix), each with clear, actionable messages.

first_principles.problem: Guardrails that only say 'denied' frustrate developers and push them to disable or bypass them.
derivation: **Preventive**: CI and admission policies with clear messages.

analogy.title: Child safety in a home
analogy.story: Socket covers (defaults), stair gates (prevention), a baby monitor (detection) and automatic shut-off on the hob (correction).
analogy.breaks: Over-strict guardrails block legitimate edge cases, so provide an exception process.

example.title: An actionable policy message

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Developers fix it in a minute without a ticket.

code.text:
✗ "admission webhook denied the request"
✓ "Container 'api' runs as root. Set securityContext.runAsNonRoot: true (see docs/security#non-root)."

example.outcome: guardrails people work with, not against.

check.q: Name the four layers of effective guardrails.
check.a: Secure defaults, preventive policies, detective controls and corrective automation.

api-design-for-platforms-intent-over-imp.core: Platform interfaces should express what developers want (a public HTTP service with a Postgres DB, scaling 2–10) rather than how it's implemented (Deployments, Services, Ingresses, IAM roles). Intent-based APIs stay stable even when the implementation changes.

first_principles.problem: Exposing raw Kubernetes and cloud resources ties every team to implementation details that later need painful migrations.
derivation: Model **intent**: workload type, exposure, dependencies, scale.
**Change the implementation** behind a stable interface.

analogy.title: Ordering in a restaurant
analogy.story: You order 'medium-rare steak', not 'heat the pan to 230°C for 3 minutes'. The kitchen can change ovens without changing the menu.
analogy.breaks: Intent APIs can't foresee every need, so pair them with escape hatches.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The platform can switch from Ingress to Gateway API with no team changes.

check.q: Why design platform APIs around intent rather than implementation?
check.a: Intent stays stable while implementations change, sparing teams from migrations and from implementation details.

the-cognitive-load-tax-why-abstraction-q.core: Every non-domain decision a developer must make (which ingress annotation, which IAM policy, which base image) is a cognitive load tax. Good abstractions remove those decisions, and the time saved compounds directly into delivery speed.

first_principles.problem: Each service requires dozens of infrastructure decisions, which slows every team and produces inconsistent results.
truths: Repeated decisions across teams multiply the waste.
derivation: **Measure**: time to first deploy, number of config fields.

analogy.title: A tax on every transaction
analogy.story: Small per-transaction taxes add up to a huge drag on the whole economy.
analogy.breaks: Removing too many choices blocks legitimate needs, so keep overrides available.

example.title: Counting the tax
flow: Time to first deploy: 3 days → 1 hour
example.outcome: abstraction quality measured in delivery speed.

check.a: The mental cost of every non-domain decision developers must make, which slows delivery across all teams.
